plot_extraction.response_text:
A narrator who loves French Canada rejects accusations that Quebec is cowardly or disloyal during the First World War and recalls several encounters that reveal the character of its people.

In 1894, guide Jean Morel tells him that if France and Britain went to war, his body would march under Britain’s flag while his heart marched under France’s. Years later, when the two nations fight together against Germany, Jean’s divided loyalty seems reconciled.

In a 1917 Oxford hospital, the narrator meets a badly wounded French-Canadian lumberjack who enlisted because Britain was defending France. Though his injured arm will prevent him from returning to woodcutting, the young man remains glad that he served and considers becoming a camp cook.

Later that year, on Quebec’s Sainte Marguerite River, the narrator questions his guide Iside about not joining the war. Iside says his priest taught that men should fight only when their own homes and churches are attacked. The narrator explains that defeating Germany abroad is necessary to preserve Canada’s liberty at home. Iside begins to understand and promises to share this broader view with his priest and community.

Finally, reports of an anti-conscription riot in Quebec City seem to confirm doubts about French-Canadian loyalty. The narrator argues, however, that the disturbance was stirred up by opportunistic politicians and hired troublemakers, not by ordinary French-Canadians. The riot quickly collapses, the draft proceeds, volunteers enlist, separatist proposals are rejected, and church leaders increasingly present the war as a Christian struggle against tyranny. The narrator concludes that Quebec’s rural people are fundamentally loyal and courageous; once properly informed about what is at stake, they will defend freedom alongside the other peoples of Canada.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the form of a personal, patriotic memoir combined with travel sketch, wartime testimony, and political essay. Its first-person narrator speaks as an educated outsider who nevertheless claims intimate knowledge of French Canada through friendship, hunting, fishing, and canoe travel. The voice is warm, confident, paternal, and morally emphatic. It begins defensively, asking the reader to suspend judgment of Quebec, and proceeds through remembered encounters intended to establish the character of ordinary French Canadians. Personal affection is presented as a basis for public argument: memories are said to be “not an argument,” yet the selected anecdotes clearly function as evidence.

The structure is episodic and retrospective. A discursive introduction is followed by four numbered, titled, and dated sections, each associated with a distinct place and moment. The sequence moves from a pre-war conversation in the wilderness to a wounded soldier in Oxford, then to wartime debate on a Quebec river, and finally to broader political commentary in Quebec City. This progression enlarges the scale from individual identity to military sacrifice, communal understanding, and national loyalty. The final section largely abandons scene-based storytelling for direct exposition and polemic, before returning at the close to the narrator’s canoemen and the emotional world of the opening.

The prose alternates between lyrical nature writing and forceful political rhetoric. Landscapes are rendered through flowing, luminous phrases such as “rushing rivers,” “sparkling lakes,” “friendly mountains,” and “luminous northern twilight.” Rivers and trees are personified as embodiments of peace, courage, liberty, and lawful order. These pastoral passages create an idealized French Canada that appears morally wholesome, stable, and remote from corrupt modern politics. By contrast, descriptions of war and Germany use harsh, inflammatory language: “ravening black eagle,” “Prussian paganism,” “thievish, brutal German hordes,” and “German criminals.” The tonal opposition is stark and characteristic of First World War propaganda: the wilderness signifies natural virtue, while German militarism signifies madness, barbarity, and spiritual corruption.

The diction is elevated but accessible, mixing literary narration with conversational directness. Long, balanced sentences carry geographical description, historical context, and political reflection, while short declarative statements deliver judgments with authority: “No!”; “That was enough”; “They are loyal by nature.” Parentheses, dashes, semicolons, exclamations, and rhetorical questions give the prose the cadence of an address delivered aloud. Repetition is used persuasively, especially in sequences such as “Do you mean to tell me…?” and in parallel lists of peoples, places, institutions, or moral values. Aphoristic formulations—“Memories would ask to be heard,” “It is the conduct that shows the Christian,” and “You have got to give them time, and light”—condense the narrator’s argument into memorable moral statements.

Dialogue is central to the anecdotal sections. The exchanges usually follow a Socratic pattern: the narrator asks leading questions, the French-Canadian speaker reveals a limited or instinctive position, and further questioning brings him toward the narrator’s broader interpretation. Speech is lightly marked by French vocabulary, translated phrases, dialect spellings, and repeated forms of address such as “M’sieu’.” Italicized French expressions and explanations of local terms lend ethnographic color and reinforce the narrator’s role as interpreter between Quebec and an English-speaking readership. The dialogue gives the woodsmen dignity, humor, sincerity, and courage, but it also portrays them paternalistically as simple, isolated, poorly informed, and dependent on educated guidance.

Characterization is economical and emblematic rather than psychologically complex. Jean Morel embodies divided cultural allegiance but practical loyalty; the wounded lumberjack represents spontaneous courage and sacrifice; Iside embodies provincial innocence capable of moral awakening; and the urban rioters serve as a negative contrast to the supposedly authentic people of forest and farm. Physical descriptions are brief and vivid—“broad-shouldered, red-bearded,” “wiry little bowman,” “fine young fellow”—and are immediately connected to moral type. The ordinary French Canadians are repeatedly associated with bodily endurance, skilled labor, family, religion, local citizenship, and closeness to nature.

The narrator frequently addresses the reader directly, creating an intimate but argumentative relationship. Phrases such as “Take them for what they are worth,” “you understand,” and the imagined intervention of the “gentle reader” allow anticipated objections to be staged and answered. The method resembles an informal courtroom defense: an accusation is introduced, witnesses are called through memory, counterarguments are acknowledged, and a favorable verdict is urged. The narrator’s professed reluctance to theorize contrasts with his extensive political conclusions, producing a style that presents ideology as common sense grounded in lived experience.

Humor appears in mild, affectionate forms. It arises from linguistic misunderstandings, practical suggestions, understated reactions, and comparisons that deflate political pretension. The riot “froths up and goes down” like ginger beer; nationalist politics becomes a soap bubble or a cinema film; the narrator hides a smile behind pipe smoke. Such humor softens the didacticism while reinforcing his superior interpretive position. Pipe-smoking, paddling, fishing, and camp conversation also create a leisurely masculine atmosphere in which serious political questions emerge naturally from outdoor companionship.

The dominant themes are loyalty, cultural duality, courage, moral education, and the relation between local identity and global duty. French-Canadian identity is treated as emotionally attached to France, politically protected by Britain, and potentially integrated into a wider imperial and Christian struggle. The story values bilingual and regional culture, but only within a larger framework of Canadian and British allegiance. Religion is judged pragmatically by conduct: the Church may either narrow its followers’ vision or awaken them to righteous sacrifice. Patriotism is defined not as blind obedience but as the defense of “justice, liberty, humanity,” though the argument remains strongly aligned with Allied wartime ideology.

Overall, the style is characteristic of early twentieth-century literary journalism and patriotic travel writing. It is scenic, anecdotal, sentimental, rhetorically assured, and openly didactic. Its strengths lie in vivid landscapes, memorable dialogue, rhythmic persuasive prose, and the fusion of private remembrance with public history. Its limitations are equally period-specific: idealization of rural people, paternalistic cultural assumptions, simplistic moral binaries, imperial confidence, and intensely dehumanizing wartime language.

# QUEBEC AND THE GREAT WAR

Before you condemn a people, you should know them.

You should have eaten their bread, heard their songs, travelled their roads, and slept beneath their roofs. Better still, you should have gone with them into the wilderness, where speech is stripped of ceremony and a man’s heart comes plainly into view beside the camp-fire.

It is easy to judge Quebec from a newspaper paragraph. A riot breaks out in a city street; a politician makes a reckless speech; a recruiting meeting fails; and immediately someone cries, “Cowards! Disloyal! Let them separate from Canada if they will not defend her!”

No! I cannot accept that verdict.

For more than twenty years I have loved French Canada—not with the enthusiasm of the tourist who sees a cathedral, buys a wooden bowl, and departs upon the evening train, but with the affection born of friendship. I have followed her rushing rivers, crossed her sparkling lakes, climbed her friendly mountains, and watched the northern twilight lingering like a benediction over her dark forests. Her canoemen have carried me through rapids; her guides have shared with me the last crust in a wet camp; her farmers have welcomed me to whitewashed kitchens where children rose politely when the stranger entered.

Memories are not arguments, perhaps. Yet memories would ask to be heard.

I remember men who could paddle from dawn to darkness, laugh at cold rain, face a wounded moose in the alder thickets, and kneel without shame when the little chapel bell sounded across the fields. Are these men cowards? I have known them to be mistaken, uninformed, suspicious of distant causes and foreign phrases. But disloyal by nature? No.

Take these recollections for what they are worth. I offer them as witnesses—not learned witnesses, not statesmen or professors, but men with axes, paddles, rifles, rosaries, and honest hands.

## I. TWO FLAGS  
### Lake Saint John Country, October 1894

Jean Morel was broad-shouldered, red-bearded, and deliberate. He wasted neither words nor matches. He could read the movement of a trout beneath brown water, smell rain before the clouds gathered, and mend a broken canoe-rib with a strip of cedar and a piece of copper wire.

For ten days he had guided me through the lake country north of Quebec. Autumn had taken possession of the forest. The birches shone pale gold; the maples burned crimson along the slopes; tamaracks stood like yellow candles among the black spruce. At evening the lakes held every colour twice, once in the sky and once in the still water, until Jean’s paddle broke the vision into widening circles.

Our last camp was pitched on a low point covered with balsam. A cold wind moved down from the north, and the fire snapped cheerfully between two stones. Jean had baked bannock in the frying-pan, and afterward we smoked in contented silence.

For some reason—perhaps because a newspaper, three weeks old, had wrapped the bacon—I began speaking of Europe. There had been one of those quarrels which statesmen manufacture from pride, suspicion, and ink. France and England, though then at peace, still looked at each other across old memories.

“Jean,” I said, “suppose France and Britain should go to war. What would you do?”

He took his pipe from his mouth and regarded me steadily.

“Why you ask me that, M’sieu’?”

“Because you are French.”

“French-Canadian,” he corrected.

“Very well. Your fathers came from France, but you live under the British flag. If the two flags were enemies, which would you follow?”

He did not answer at once. The firelight moved over his strong face. Beyond him the lake whispered against the stones, a peaceful sound in a peaceful land.

“At the church,” he said slowly, “we pray for the Queen.”

“Yes.”

“And my grandfather, he say the English law is good law. A man keep his farm. He keep his religion. Nobody make him speak English to the bon Dieu.”

“That is true.”

“But France—” He paused, searching for words. “France is like the old mother. We do not see her. We do not know her now. But we have the songs. My mother sing them. We have the names, the saints, the stories. When the people speak of France, something move here.”

He laid one rough hand upon his breast.

“Then you would fight for France?”

He shook his head impatiently.

“I am Canadian. If war come, my country call me under the British flag. My body, he march there.”

“And your heart?”

Again the hand touched his breast.

“My heart—he march with France.”

There it was: the whole problem in a woodsman’s sentence. Political allegiance upon one side, inherited affection upon the other; duty pointing westward, memory eastward. I thought then it was a tragic division.

Years passed. Kings died, ministries changed, and the world called itself civilized. Then the storm burst. Germany struck through Belgium, France stood in peril, and Britain drew the sword beside her.

I remembered Jean Morel.

Somewhere, if he still lived, that red-bearded guide must have heard the chapel bell ring news of war across the Laurentian fields. At last his two processions had joined. His body could march under Britain’s flag while his heart marched openly with France. Duty and affection went down the same road.

Surely such a man could understand the call. Surely thousands like him could understand it—if only the truth reached them plainly, not smothered beneath party cries and the dust raised by clever tongues.

## II. THE MAN IN THE BLUE COAT  
### Oxford, March 1917

In the spring of 1917 I visited a hospital at Oxford. It occupied a group of buildings never designed for suffering. Outside, ancient towers rose tranquilly above lawns touched with the first green of the year. Bells measured the hours as they had measured them for centuries. Within were rows of narrow beds, the odour of antiseptics, the soft steps of nurses, and the terrible patience of broken youth.

There were Englishmen from the Somme, Australians from Gallipoli, Canadians from Ypres, and men whose bodies carried fragments of places that would remain forever obscure to history. Each bed seemed a little frontier between hope and darkness.

A nurse stopped me beside a young fellow in a faded blue dressing-gown.

“He is from Quebec,” she said. “Perhaps you can talk to him.”

His face was pale beneath a shock of dark hair. One arm lay outside the blanket, strong and brown; the other was hidden beneath a rigid framework of bandages. His name was Étienne Gagnon, and his home was near the upper Saint-Maurice.

“You are a lumberman?” I asked.

He smiled.

“Yes, M’sieu’. In winter I cut. In spring I drive the logs. Sometimes in summer I work for the club—carry canoe, make camp, show gentlemen where the trout do not bite.”

“That last must require great skill.”

“Ah, yes! The gentleman, he must believe always the big trout is in the next pool.”

The nurse laughed and moved away.

“How did you come here, Étienne?”

“By train, then by ship.”

“I mean, why did you enlist?”

His expression suggested that the question was unnecessarily complicated.

“Britain was fighting for France.”

“That was enough?”

“Certainly. The Germans were in France. They burn houses, break churches, push the people away. My father say, ‘If I am young, I go.’ He is not young. So I go.”

“Did your priest approve?”

“Our old curé say nothing against. He bless me. My mother cry much; afterward she is proud. She send me a scapular, but the shell does not respect it very well.”

He glanced toward the imprisoned arm.

“What happened?”

“At Courcelette. We go over in the morning. There is smoke, noise—everything mixed. My captain fall. Then a shell come close, too close. I wake in a place under the ground. After that, many trains, many doctors, much soup.”

“Will the arm recover?”

The humour faded, though not the courage.

“The doctor say I keep it. That is good. But the elbow will not bend much, perhaps. The fingers—two of them do not obey.”

“And you were right-handed?”

“Yes.”

I looked at the visible arm. The wrist was thin, but the muscles still told of axe and paddle.

“What will you do when you go home?”

He considered.

“To cut timber, maybe no. A man cannot swing axe with one arm asleep. To drive logs, also difficult. The river does not wait when you say, ‘Please, my bad hand!’”

He smiled again, but his eyes had turned toward the window.

“Do you regret going?”

His head came round quickly.

“No, M’sieu’!”

The answer rang out so sharply that a soldier in the next bed stirred.

Étienne lowered his voice. “I regret only that I cannot go back. France is not free yet. The war is not finish.”

“But you have paid heavily.”

“All pay something. Some pay everything.”

“What will become of you?”

“My brother write that perhaps I make cook in lumber camp. The cook use two hands, yes, but he have helpers. I can order them with one.” He lifted his sound hand like a commander directing an army. “Also I know beans. Nobody can defeat a man who knows beans.”

We both laughed. Then he said quietly:

“A man does not need two good arms to be glad he has done his duty.”

That was all. No speech, no theory of empire, no hatred. He had seen France attacked; Britain had defended her; Canada had called; and he had gone. The reasoning was as direct as a wood road.

When I left the ward, the evening bells were sounding over Oxford. Their music seemed to mingle with another sound in my mind—the stroke of axes in the snowy forests of Quebec.

Tell me that province has given too few men, if you must. Tell me recruiting was mishandled, that suspicion was allowed to grow, that the appeal came in words unfamiliar to the habitant. But do not tell me there was no courage in Étienne Gagnon.

I have seen his face.

## III. ISIDE LEARNS THE SIZE OF HIS HOUSE  
### Sainte Marguerite River, September 1917

That autumn I went to the Sainte Marguerite for salmon. The river ran clear and cold between wooded hills, now grave with the first touch of frost. Here and there a maple flung out its scarlet banner. The spruces stood dark and faithful along the banks, and above them the sky widened into that luminous northern blue which seems to promise both peace and courage.

My bowman was Iside Lavoie, a wiry little man with quick black eyes. He could slip a canoe through broken water as neatly as a needle through cloth. He knew every stone in the river and had a name for each pool—some names belonging to saints, others to old accidents, and a few not suitable for Sunday.

One afternoon we rested below a rapid. The canoe lay on the shingle, and Iside crouched by a small fire, boiling tea black enough to stain a paddle. The war had been much in my thoughts.

“Iside,” I asked, “how old are you?”

“Twenty-seven, M’sieu’.”

“Married?”

“Yes. Three children. The smallest is very loud.”

“And you are strong?”

He looked at me suspiciously. “Strong enough for the canoe.”

“Why are you not in the army?”

He stirred the tea, though it needed no stirring.

“My cousin Alcide is gone.”

“I asked about you.”

“My wife need me.”

“So did the wives of other men.”

He frowned. “The curé say a man fight when his own country is attack. If somebody come to burn our church, take our farm, hurt our women—then I fight. But this war is far away. It belongs to kings.”

“Does it?”

“That is what we hear.”

“Who tells you?”

“People. The newspaper. Men in the village.”

“What men?”

He waved toward the forest, as if politicians were hidden among the spruces. “Men who know.”

“That is a dangerous tribe, Iside.”

He grinned, but said nothing.

“Suppose,” I continued, “a man begins to set fire to a house at the other end of your village. Do you wait until the flames reach your own roof?”

“If there are people inside, I help.”

“Even if it is not your house?”

“Certainly.”

“Why?”

“Because it is Christian.”

“Good. Suppose a thief attacks your neighbour on the road. Do you wait until he has finished and comes for you?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because then he is stronger. Also my neighbour may be my friend.”

“Exactly. Belgium was a little neighbour attacked upon the road. France was a house set on fire. Britain went to help. Canada belongs to the same family and enjoys the liberty protected by that family. Yet you tell me the affair is none of ours.”

Iside poured tea into two tin cups. His face was thoughtful.

“But Canada is not attack.”

“Not yet, perhaps. Do you imagine the ocean is a wall which no army, no fleet, no ambition can cross? Do you think liberty lives without defenders? If Germany conquered France and broke Britain, how long would Canada remain free to govern herself, keep her language, protect her church, and raise her children in peace?”

He glanced instinctively upstream. Beyond a bend lay the valley where his home stood.

“They would come here?”

“Perhaps not tomorrow in grey uniforms. Tyranny does not always arrive at the front door with a drum. First it destroys the friends who might help you. Then it controls the seas, the trade, the laws, the future. Your house, Iside, is larger than the cabin where your children sleep.”

He looked puzzled.

“Larger?”

“Your house is Canada. Its road reaches to the ocean. Its safety is joined to the safety of free nations. When France is struck, something in your house is struck. When Britain stands between you and danger, you owe her more than a prayer.”

The river spoke beside us, running with that composed strength which comes from many hidden springs. Iside watched it for a while.

“Our curé is a good man,” he said.

“I do not doubt it.”

“He care for the poor. When my little girl is sick, he come in snow.”

“Then speak to him respectfully.”

“You think he does not understand?”

“I think he may not have been told the whole truth. Many good men see only the field before their door. Show them the road beyond it.”

He sipped the tea and made a face—not because it was bitter, for he preferred it so, but because thought had become uncomfortable.

“The politicians say the English want to make us fight for England.”

“Some politicians would say the moon was made of cheese if they owned the cheese shop. Forget them. Ask yourself what England is fighting for now. Ask what happened to Belgium. Ask why Étienne Gagnon, a lumberman from the Saint-Maurice, lies with a shattered arm in an Oxford hospital.”

I told him about Étienne. Iside listened without interruption.

“At Courcelette?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“My wife’s cousin die there.”

“And was he defending nothing?”

The little bowman leaned forward, elbows upon knees.

“No. Not nothing.”

“Was he less a Canadian because he died in France?”

“No.”

“Was he a fool?”

Iside’s eyes flashed. “No, M’sieu’! He was brave.”

“Then perhaps bravery sees a danger before it reaches the church door.”

For a long minute there was only the rush of water over stones.

At last he said, “I will talk to the curé.”

“Do that.”

“And to Baptiste, who has seven sons.”

“Talk first to the sons. Baptiste may hide them in the hay.”

Iside laughed. “He hide nothing. His wife find it.”

Then his face grew serious again.

“I cannot promise I go. There is my wife, the children, the old mother. But I promise this: I tell what you say. The house is larger. The fire at the other end may come to us.”

“That is enough for one afternoon.”

We launched the canoe. Iside took his place in the bow, and the paddle entered the water without a splash. Above us the river narrowed between high banks, free and shining, obedient to its ancient channel yet always moving toward a wider world.

You have got to give men time, and light. A truth shouted in a strange language often sounds like an insult. The same truth spoken beside their own river may sound like duty.

## IV. THE FROTH AND THE CURRENT  
### Quebec City, Easter 1918

Then came the disturbance in Quebec City.

The reports travelled quickly: crowds in the streets, windows broken, offices attacked, soldiers summoned, shots fired, men killed. To many Canadians it appeared that the mask had fallen at last.

“There!” they said. “What more proof do you need? Quebec will not obey the law. Quebec is false to Canada.”

The accusation was understandable. It was also unjust.

A riot is noisy; loyalty commonly works in silence. One broken window makes more news than a thousand farms where men rise before daylight, pay their taxes, pray for sons overseas, and obey laws they do not altogether like. A crowd beneath electric lamps is easily photographed. Character in a distant parish is not.

Let us be honest. Conscription was bitterly disliked in much of Quebec. Recruiting had failed there in painful measure. Certain newspapers had fed distrust; certain speakers had whispered that the war was merely an English quarrel; certain political adventurers had discovered that fear, when stirred vigorously, brings votes to the surface.

But who made the riot?

Was it Jean Morel, weighing old France and present duty beside a northern fire? Was it Étienne Gagnon, offering his good arm and receiving a ruined one in return? Was it Iside Lavoie, slowly learning that the safety of his children might depend upon battles beyond the sea?

No.

The disturbance was the work of a mixed and inflammable crowd—boys hunting excitement, idlers hunting plunder, agitators hunting influence, and hired roughs hunting anything that could be smashed. Honest anxiety was present, no doubt; so was anger. But opportunists supplied the matches.

Such outbreaks froth up and go down like ginger beer. For an hour the bottle seems all foam. Presently the foam sinks, and one discovers how little substance it contained.

The riot collapsed. The law remained. Registration continued. The draft proceeded. Men obeyed who had declared they never would. Others volunteered rather than wait. Quebec did not secede, burn her churches, renounce Canada, or invite a foreign flag above her citadel.

Indeed, when a few zealots proposed a separate state, their grand scheme rose like a soap bubble, glittered with every colour of rhetoric, and burst at the touch of practical sense. The farmer wanted better roads, a fair price for his crop, schools for his children, and peace for his parish. He did not want a paper republic manufactured in a back room by gentlemen who had never guided a canoe through a rapid or brought hay in before a storm.

Separation sounds magnificent in a speech. It looks less attractive when one asks who will pay the railway debt.

More important still, the moral meaning of the war was becoming clearer. The Church, slow in some quarters and cautious in others, began to speak with a stronger voice. Priests who once had treated the conflict as a distant quarrel now saw the burned sanctuaries of Belgium, the ravaged homes of France, and the claim of militarism to master the conscience of mankind. Bishops called upon their people to recognize that justice also has a flag, and that Christianity cannot remain neutral when power tramples the weak.

It is the conduct that shows the Christian.

A man may cross himself at every roadside shrine, but if he will not lift a hand while his neighbour is robbed, his devotion has become an ornament. Another man may stumble over the words of doctrine, yet if he gives his strength to defend the oppressed, something of the true faith burns within him.

This lesson reached Quebec—not everywhere at once, not in the same form, and not without resistance. Truth travels slowly along country roads. But it travels.

The habitant began to understand that Britain had not entered the struggle merely to enlarge an empire; that France was not fighting for glory; that Canada’s sacrifice was not demanded for the amusement of kings. Behind the smoke and wire stood a plain question: Should nations live by law or by force? Should a treaty bind the strong as well as the weak? Should a small people be allowed its home, its language, and its worship—or should these things endure only until some armed master desired otherwise?

Put the matter that way to French Canada and you touch her own history. She knows what language means. She knows what religion means. She knows the value of laws which protect a minority. Ask her to die for an abstraction called imperial policy, and she may turn away. Ask her to defend the right of a people to remain itself, and she begins to listen.

Some will say, “You excuse too much. Other provinces understood sooner.”

Perhaps. Other provinces heard the appeal in their own political vocabulary. Their newspapers explained the cause; their schools had taught them the history behind it; their public men spoke in familiar terms. Quebec was too often addressed by scolding. When she hesitated, accusation replaced persuasion. Men told her she was disloyal before they had taken the trouble to tell her clearly what loyalty required.

There is no virtue in ignorance. But neither is there wisdom in insulting the ignorant.

The rural French Canadian is conservative in the deepest meaning of that word. He clings to family, field, parish, language, and inherited custom. He mistrusts sudden commands from distant offices. He asks, “Will this injure my children? Will it take away what my fathers preserved?” These instincts may narrow his horizon, but they do not make him a traitor. They are the roots from which loyalty grows, once he understands that the larger country shelters the smaller home.

He is loyal by nature—to what he knows.

The task is to enlarge his knowledge without mocking his affections. Tell him that Canada asks him to cease being French, and he will resist. Tell him that Canada needs the courage of its French sons precisely because their heritage is precious, and he will stand straighter. Show him France in danger, Britain defending the law, Belgium crucified for keeping faith, and Canada summoned to protect the liberty under which all her peoples live—and the road opens before him.

I do not pretend every Jean became a soldier, every Étienne a hero, every Iside a convert. Human beings are not symbols marching neatly in a parade. There were cowards in Quebec, as there were cowards in Ontario, Scotland, Australia, and every land that sent brave men to battle. There were selfish farmers, dishonest contractors, noisy demagogues, timid priests, and young men who preferred safety.

But cowardice is personal, not provincial. Disloyalty has no mother tongue.

When I think of Quebec, I do not first see the Easter crowd swirling through the narrow streets beneath the old walls. I see a red-bearded guide beside an autumn lake, his body pledged to Britain and his heart faithful to France. I see a pale lumberjack in a blue hospital coat, planning to command a kitchen with one hand because the other had been broken in the defence of freedom. I see a wiry bowman crouched beside the Sainte Marguerite, troubled by the sudden discovery that his house was larger than he had dreamed.

And behind them I see the long procession of the quiet people: farmers turning the dark soil, women reading letters from overseas, priests speaking beneath wooden crucifixes, children learning two histories that may yet become one. Above them are the Laurentian hills; before them, the great river; around them, the forests breathing their ancient lesson of endurance.

The river does not cease to be itself because tributaries enter it. It gathers them, carries them, and grows strong.

So Canada must gather her peoples—not by crushing memory, not by ridiculing difference, not by calling one race loyal and another suspect, but by showing all of them the common channel in which their freedom runs.

Give Quebec truth instead of taunts. Give her time, and light. Speak to her in the language of justice, liberty, humanity, and faith. Then, when danger comes near enough to be clearly seen, the men of her farms and forests will not hide behind their mountains.

They will take the paddle, the axe, the rifle—whatever duty places in their hands—and go with the others.

I know them.

# The Library of Unsent Letters

Every morning at eight, Mara Vale unlocked the narrow blue door between the bakery and the watchmaker’s shop and entered a room full of things people had never said.

The room was officially called the Municipal Archive of Undeliverable Correspondence. The brass plate beside the door said so in letters too small for anyone to read without leaning close. Most people in Bellwether simply called it the Library of Unsent Letters.

It was not, strictly speaking, a library. Nothing could be borrowed. Nothing could be copied. The letters arrived in sacks from post offices across the country: envelopes without addresses, envelopes addressed to the dead, envelopes found in demolished houses or discovered at the bottoms of old mailboxes. Some had stamps but no names. Some had names but no towns. A few were blank outside and filled within.

Mara catalogued them all.

She worked alone beneath a green glass lamp, recording the date, paper, ink, condition, and any identifying details. Then she placed each letter in an acid-free sleeve and filed it by year.

She never read more than necessary.

That was the first rule.

The second rule was that no letter could leave the archive.

Mara had kept both rules for eleven years.

Then, on a rainy Tuesday in November, she found a letter addressed to herself.

The envelope lay on top of a canvas mail sack from the abandoned North Bellwether Post Office. It was cream-colored, sealed with blue wax, and marked by a dark stain in one corner. Her name had been written across the front in black ink.

MARA VALE  
THE BLUE DOOR  
BELLWETHER

There was no stamp.

She stood perfectly still, listening to rain tick against the window.

Very few people knew she worked behind the blue door. Fewer still wrote letters. Her father had died when she was nineteen, her mother two years later, and her older brother, Tomas, had vanished at sea before either of them.

Her friends had gradually become holiday cards, then names in an address book she no longer opened.

Mara turned the envelope over.

The blue wax seal bore the impression of a moth.

Her brother had owned a brass seal exactly like it.

She sat down.

For a long time she did nothing. The archive seemed to breathe around her: paper settling, shelves creaking, rain whispering in the chimney. On her desk, the letter waited with the patience of something that had already crossed a great distance.

At last, Mara broke the seal.

Inside was a single sheet.

Dear Mara,

If this reaches you, the tide has begun to turn.

I am sorry it took me so long to write. I am sorrier that I cannot tell you where I have been, because I do not yet know where “here” is.

Do you remember the summer we found the staircase beneath the cliffs? You said it led nowhere. I said every staircase leads somewhere, even if the place has forgotten its name.

You were right to be afraid.

I was wrong to go back alone.

If you still have the red compass, bring it to the old lighthouse before midnight on the first snow. Do not let the bell ring thirteen times.

Your brother,  
Tomas

Mara read it twice.

Then she examined the paper.

The watermark belonged to a mill that had closed twenty-six years ago. The ink was iron gall. The handwriting was Tomas’s—she knew the slant of it, the long crossbars on his t’s, the way his lowercase r looked unfinished.

But Tomas had disappeared seventeen years earlier.

His boat, the Ardent, had been found drifting three miles beyond the harbor. Its sail was torn. Its lantern was still burning. There was no blood, no sign of struggle, and no body.

Only the red compass had remained, tucked beneath a coil of rope.

Mara had kept it in a cedar box under her bed.

That evening, she carried the letter home inside her coat.

It was the first rule she broke.

The snow began just after sunset.

At first it melted on the cobblestones, but by nine o’clock the roofs had whitened. Bellwether grew quiet. Shopkeepers turned their signs and drew their curtains. The harbor foghorn groaned beyond the dark houses.

Mara sat at her kitchen table with the red compass before her.

It did not point north.

It never had.

The needle drifted aimlessly, circling whenever she moved the brass case. As children, Tomas had claimed it pointed toward whatever had been lost most recently. Mara had called that nonsense.

Now the needle held steady toward the eastern cliffs.

Toward the lighthouse.

She put on her boots.

The lighthouse had been abandoned since the new electric beacon was built across the bay. It stood above the cliffs like a pale finger raised in warning. The path to it twisted through thorn bushes and wind-bent grass.

By the time Mara reached the iron gate, snow had gathered on her shoulders.

The gate was unlocked.

Beyond it, the lighthouse door hung open.

“Tomas?” she called.

Only the sea answered.

Mara stepped inside.

The circular room smelled of salt and rust. A spiral staircase climbed into darkness. On the wall, someone had scratched hundreds of short lines into the plaster, grouped in sets of twelve.

At the center of the floor stood a wooden desk.

A letter waited on it.

Mara approached slowly.

The envelope was addressed to Elias Venn, Bellwether Watchmaker.

She knew Elias. His shop stood beside the archive. He was a quiet man in his sixties who repaired clocks no one else would touch. They exchanged polite greetings every morning. Sometimes he left a paper cup of coffee outside her door.

The envelope had already been opened.

Mara removed the letter.

Dear Elias,

You will tell yourself that silence is kindness. It is not.

When the bell stops, take the stairs beneath the lighthouse. Bring the key you found in your father’s coat.

You have been waiting for permission.

Here it is.

The letter was unsigned.

Above her, a mechanism groaned.

Mara looked up.

The lighthouse bell rang once.

Its voice rolled through the tower, deep and enormous.

The red compass spun in her hand.

Then it pointed toward the floor.

Mara knelt and brushed aside dust. Beneath the desk was an iron ring set into a circular trapdoor.

She pulled.

The door opened on blackness and the smell of cold stone. Steps descended below the lighthouse.

The bell rang a second time.

Mara thought of the letter to Elias. She thought of Tomas’s warning. Then she lowered the trapdoor and ran back into the snow.

The watchmaker’s shop was dark, but Elias answered after her third knock. He wore a brown dressing gown and held a fireplace poker.

“Mara?”

She pushed the letter toward him. “Did you write this?”

His face changed before he touched it.

“Where did you find it?”

“At the lighthouse.”

Elias read the letter beneath the porch light. When he finished, he sat down heavily on the doorstep.

The bell rang again in the distance.

Three.

“You know about the stairs,” Mara said.

Elias folded the letter with trembling care. “My father called them the Downward Road.”

“What is that?”

“A story.”

“I don’t have time for stories.”

“Stories are what people call the truth when it frightens them.”

The bell rang a fourth time.

Elias looked toward the cliffs.

“My father maintained the old lighthouse,” he said. “He claimed the tower was built over something much older—a place where lost things gathered. Not misplaced things. Lost things. Ships that sailed into fog and never returned. Roads erased from maps. Names no living person remembered.”

“People?”

Elias looked at her. “Sometimes.”

Mara’s fingers tightened around the compass.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because your brother made me promise.”

The world seemed to tilt beneath her.

“You saw Tomas?”

“The night he vanished. He came to my shop soaked to the skin, though there had been no rain. He asked about the lighthouse. I told him what my father had told me.” Elias shut his eyes. “I thought he wanted a sailor’s tale. By the time I realized he believed me, he had gone.”

The bell rang a fifth time.

“What happens at thirteen?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

“You have a key?”

Elias hesitated, then nodded.

He dressed quickly. From a drawer behind the shop counter, he took a long black key spotted with rust.

They crossed town together.

Snow fell thickly now, swallowing their footprints almost as soon as they made them. No lights shone in the houses. The whole town appeared abandoned, preserved beneath glass.

As they reached the lighthouse, the bell rang six.

Inside, the trapdoor stood open.

“I closed that,” Mara whispered.

A dim blue light rose from below.

Elias unlocked a small gate at the foot of the stairs. Beyond it, the passage descended through wet rock.

They began to climb down.

The bell rang seven times.

The sound followed them underground.

The staircase spiraled deeper than the height of the cliff. Water shone on the walls, though Mara could not hear the sea. As they descended, they passed objects resting on the steps: a child’s shoe, a silver spoon, a violin with no strings, a cracked photograph in which every face had faded.

“Don’t touch anything,” Elias warned.

At the bottom, the staircase opened into a vast chamber.

Mara lifted her lamp.

Shelves extended into the darkness.

They were filled with letters.

Thousands upon thousands of envelopes rested in stone alcoves or lay stacked in drifts across the floor. Letters hung from roots in the ceiling. Letters floated in pools of black water without sinking. Some looked ancient; others were bright and new.

Mara moved closer to the nearest shelf.

Every envelope bore a name.

Ada Rowe. Samuel Pike. Lillian Marr. Oren Vale.

Her father’s name.

She reached for it.

Elias caught her wrist. “Don’t.”

“That’s my father.”

“No. That is a letter to your father.”

The distinction stopped her.

All around them, paper rustled though there was no wind.

“What is this place?” she asked.

“A post office,” said a voice in the darkness. “Of a sort.”

A man stepped between the shelves.

He was tall and thin, dressed in a dark uniform with silver buttons. A mailbag hung from one shoulder. His face was pale, his hair white, but his eyes were those of someone much younger.

On his chest was a brass badge.

POSTMASTER, it read.

“You are late,” he said.

“For what?” Mara asked.

“To collect what belongs to you.”

He reached into his bag and withdrew a bundle of letters tied with blue thread.

All were addressed to Mara.

She saw her mother’s handwriting. Her father’s. Tomas’s. Some she did not recognize. One envelope bore her own writing, though she had never seen it before.

“I don’t understand.”

“Most letters are not lost because the destination cannot be found,” the Postmaster said. “They are lost because the sender lacks courage. A confession burned before dawn. An apology folded but never sent. A farewell spoken only in the mind. Such words must go somewhere.”

“So they come here?”

“Eventually.”

The bell rang eight times.

Dust drifted from the ceiling.

The Postmaster glanced upward. “The road is closing.”

“Where is my brother?” Mara asked.

The Postmaster studied her. “Further in.”

“Take me to him.”

“I cannot.”

“Then tell me the way.”

“There is no way further in. Only a reason.”

Mara stepped toward him. “I have crossed half the town in a snowstorm, climbed under a lighthouse, and found a dead post office full of letters that were never written. I am finished with riddles.”

For the first time, the Postmaster smiled.

“You are very like him.”

The bell rang nine.

A crack split one of the stone shelves. Letters spilled out, fluttering like startled birds.

Elias stared upward. “What happens when the bell rings thirteen times?”

“The archive closes,” said the Postmaster.

“For how long?”

“Until it is forgotten again.”

Mara looked at the countless shelves. “And anyone still inside?”

“Becomes part of the collection.”

Elias gripped his key. “We should go.”

“I’m not leaving without Tomas.”

“Mara—”

“He is alive.”

The Postmaster’s expression did not change.

“You know he is,” she said.

“He is not dead.”

Hope struck her so sharply it felt like pain.

“Where?”

The Postmaster pointed to the red compass. “It has always known.”

Mara opened her hand.

The needle turned toward a narrow passage between the shelves.

She ran.

The passage twisted through chambers crowded with undelivered words. She heard Elias behind her, calling her name, and the Postmaster’s calm voice warning that time was short.

The bell rang ten.

The shelves began to shake.

Envelopes burst open as they fell. Murmurs filled the air: apologies, declarations, accusations, final blessings. Thousands of voices spoke at once.

I should have stayed.

I never blamed you.

The money is beneath the floor.

You were the bravest person I knew.

Please forgive me.

I love you.

I love you.

I love you.

Mara covered her ears and followed the compass.

The passage ended at an underground shore.

A black sea stretched beyond sight. There was no wind, but waves moved slowly across it, reflecting stars that could not possibly be overhead.

A wooden boat waited in the shallows.

A man sat inside.

His hair had gone gray at the temples. His coat was worn. A brass moth seal hung on a chain around his neck.

Mara stopped breathing.

“Tomas.”

He looked up.

For a moment neither of them moved.

Then he climbed from the boat and stumbled through the water. Mara met him at the shore. He wrapped his arms around her, and she felt the solid truth of him—his wet coat, his shaking shoulders, his hand against the back of her head.

“You got the letter,” he said.

She pulled away and struck him across the face.

The sound echoed over the water.

“That,” she said, “was for seventeen years.”

He touched his cheek. “Fair.”

She embraced him again.

The bell rang eleven.

Elias reached the shore, breathless. “We need to leave now.”

Tomas looked toward the passage. “The door is closing?”

“Yes.”

“Then go.”

Mara stared at him. “We are going.”

“I can’t.”

“You can explain on the stairs.”

Tomas shook his head. “The boat needs a keeper. Someone has to carry the letters across.”

“Across to where?”

“Where they need to go.”

The black sea moved behind him. Far away, faint lights drifted like lanterns.

“The old Postmaster lied to me,” Tomas continued. “He said I could go home when another keeper came. But no one comes here by choice.”

Mara thought of the pale man and his mailbag. “He said the letters were mine.”

“They are bait,” Tomas said. “The archive finds what you most want to hear.”

The bell rang twelve.

The chamber shuddered. Stone broke somewhere in the distance.

Elias seized Mara’s arm. “Now.”

She pulled free. “There has to be another way.”

“There is,” said the Postmaster.

He stood at the entrance to the shore.

Behind him, letters spun through the passage in a white storm.

Tomas stepped in front of Mara. “You.”

The Postmaster removed his cap.

Without it, he seemed older than the lighthouse, older than Bellwether, perhaps older than the habit of naming things one could not understand.

“A letter received is a door closed,” he said. “A letter answered is a door opened. One of you may leave. One must remain. Unless the final letter is delivered.”

He pointed to the bundle in Mara’s hand.

She had forgotten she carried it.

The letters tied in blue thread.

“What final letter?” she asked.

“The one in your own hand.”

Mara untied the bundle. The envelope written by her rested at the bottom.

On its front were the words:

TO THE ONE I LEFT BEHIND

The paper felt warm.

She opened it.

Inside was a blank sheet.

“I didn’t write this.”

“Not yet,” said the Postmaster.

The tower groaned above them.

The first stroke of the thirteenth bell began.

Its sound was lower than the others, slow and vast.

Mara understood.

She took Elias’s fountain pen from his coat pocket. Kneeling on the stone shore, she placed the blank paper on the envelope.

“What do I write?”

“The truth,” Tomas said.

The bell continued to sound.

Mara set the pen to the page.

For years she had believed silence protected her. She had never told her father she blamed him for letting Tomas sail in bad weather. She had never told her mother she planned to leave Bellwether, because her mother died before Mara found the courage. She had never told Tomas that on the morning he vanished, she had seen him preparing the Ardent and refused to speak to him.

They had argued the night before.

Tomas wanted to return to the staircase beneath the cliffs. Mara called him selfish, childish, obsessed. He told her she was afraid of everything that could not be catalogued.

When she saw him at the harbor the next morning, she turned away.

For seventeen years, she had imagined that if she had called his name, he would have stayed.

She began to write.

Dear Tomas,

I have spent half my life being angry with you because anger was easier to carry than grief.

I told myself you abandoned us. I told myself you chose a mystery over your family. The truth is that I saw you leave, and I let my pride keep me silent.

I thought silence made me innocent.

It did not.

But I will not trade my life for yours, and I will not allow you to trade yours for mine. Whatever debt exists between us, I forgive it. Whatever words we failed to say, we will say them now.

You are not the one I left behind.

I am.

Mara signed her name.

The moment she finished, the paper folded itself.

The envelope sealed with blue wax.

Across its front appeared a name.

MARA VALE

The thirteenth bell fell silent before completing its first stroke.

The underground sea rose.

A wave rushed toward the shore, black and filled with stars. Tomas grabbed Mara’s hand. Elias caught Tomas’s coat.

The wave struck.

For an instant, Mara was underwater.

Letters surrounded her, no longer made of paper but of light. Their voices passed through her—not words exactly, but intentions: sorrow seeking forgiveness, love seeking witness, truth seeking a place to rest.

Then the world turned over.

Mara awoke in the lighthouse.

Morning light streamed through broken windows. Snow lay across the floor.

Elias was beside her, coughing.

Tomas lay near the open door.

Mara crawled to him and pressed two fingers to his throat.

A pulse answered.

Outside, Bellwether shone beneath the snow.

The trapdoor was gone. In its place lay a smooth circle of stone.

On the desk rested a single envelope addressed to Mara.

She opened it.

Inside was the letter she had written on the underground shore. Beneath her signature, another line had appeared in Tomas’s hand.

I forgive you, too.

They walked back to town after sunrise.

No one saw them at first. Then the baker opened her shutters and dropped a tray of rolls. A fisherman recognized Tomas and crossed himself. By the time they reached the harbor, half the town had gathered behind them.

There were questions, of course.

Where had he been?

How had he survived?

Why had he not aged seventeen years?

Tomas tried to answer honestly.

He said he had been delivering letters across a sea beneath the world.

Most people decided the experience had confused him. A few believed every word. The rest accepted uncertainty, as people in harbor towns often must.

Elias returned to his clocks.

Tomas moved into Mara’s spare room and slept for three days.

As for the Library of Unsent Letters, it changed.

The sacks stopped arriving from distant post offices. The shelves remained, but sometimes letters vanished from their sleeves. Mara would find them gone in the morning, leaving only a faint trace of salt.

Other letters appeared beneath the blue door.

These were not old.

They came from the people of Bellwether.

A confession from the baker to her estranged daughter. An apology from the mayor to his brother. A love letter from a schoolteacher who had postponed love for thirty years.

Mara no longer catalogued them.

Instead, she delivered them.

Some recipients wept. Some laughed. Some tore the letters in half. A few wrote answers.

All were better than silence.

Years later, when the blue door needed repainting, Tomas helped her remove it from its hinges. Beneath the flaking paint, they found dozens of names carved into the wood. Neither recognized them.

At the very bottom was the shape of a moth.

“Do you think the archive is still down there?” Tomas asked.

Mara considered the question.

The old lighthouse had collapsed during a spring storm. Nothing remained on the cliff but white stones and a rusted bell.

“Somewhere,” she said.

Tomas held up the red compass.

The needle no longer wandered. It pointed steadily toward the blue door.

“Still broken,” he said.

“No,” Mara replied. “I think it finally knows what was lost.”

Together they rehung the door.

The next morning, Mara arrived at eight and found an envelope waiting on the step. It had no stamp, no address, and no name.

Inside was a single blank page.

Once, she would have filed it away.

Instead, she placed it on the desk beside a bottle of ink and left the door open.

Outside, Bellwether woke beneath a clear sky. The bakery filled the street with the smell of warm bread. Elias raised the shutters of the watchmaker’s shop. In the harbor, Tomas stood on the deck of a newly painted boat, calling to fishermen as gulls wheeled above him.

Someone paused at the open blue door.

Mara did not look up immediately. She gave the visitor time.

At last, a woman entered. She was young, perhaps twenty, with rain on her coat though the day was dry. Her hands trembled.

“I was told,” the woman said, “that this is where people bring things they don’t know how to say.”

Mara pushed the blank page toward her.

“It used to be,” she said.

“And now?”

“Now it is where they learn to say them.”
